# Database engines (experimental)
Source: https://docs.openclaw.ai/reference/database-engines

OpenClaw uses SQLite by default. The experimental PostgreSQL adapter lets one
Gateway keep supported stores in PostgreSQL while other stores stay on SQLite.
The adapter owns connection setup, schema admission, transaction behavior, and
commit notifications; stores keep their existing data and operation contracts.

Daemon runtime pins stay local on every engine, in
`<state-root>/control/services.sqlite`. The daemon owner supplies typed runtime
intent to the macOS app without requiring a running Gateway or PostgreSQL
connection. Shared-state engine selection does not move this store.
No release stored runtime pins in PostgreSQL shared state, so PostgreSQL installs have no legacy pin source to migrate.

## Configure PostgreSQL

Use a PostgreSQL database and a role that can create schemas
and tables. PostgreSQL 16 or newer and UTF8 server and client encoding are required;
admission checks these once per physical store load. No extensions are installed
by the engine. Put its connection DSN in a secret, then configure a SecretRef:

```json5
{
  database: {
    engine: "postgres",
    postgres: {
      connection: { source: "env", provider: "default", id: "OPENCLAW_DATABASE_DSN" },
      schemaPrefix: "openclaw",
    },
  },
}
```

Provide `OPENCLAW_DATABASE_DSN` in the Gateway's environment through your secret
manager. It is the secret referenced by this example, not an engine-selection
environment variable. [File and exec references](/gateway/secrets/secretref-contract)
are also supported. Store-backed references are rejected because resolving them
requires the shared database that this connection must open. Use an env, file or
exec SecretRef instead; `openclaw doctor` reports invalid connection refs.
The host resolves the secret and passes the connection to
database workers; workers do not resolve SecretRefs. Treat the DSN as a credential
and do not put it in logs or diagnostic captures.

Restart the Gateway after changing the engine, then run `openclaw doctor` to see
each store's selected engine. Doctor warns that PostgreSQL is experimental and
that stores without a PostgreSQL schema remain on SQLite.

| Field                            | Default      | Meaning                                                                                                                                                          |
| -------------------------------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `database.engine`                | `"sqlite"`   | `"sqlite"` or `"postgres"`. PostgreSQL applies to every registered store that supplies a PostgreSQL schema.                                                      |
| `database.postgres.connection`   | None         | Required for PostgreSQL. A DSN string or env/file/exec SecretRef; store-backed refs are rejected.                                                                |
| `database.postgres.schemaPrefix` | `"openclaw"` | Prefix for new store schemas: 1–27 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores, starting with a letter or underscore. Existing anchors keep their recorded schema. |

Shared state, agent databases, Workboard, Logbook, and Team Reports currently support PostgreSQL. The Gateway resolves
the selected engine before its first shared-state read and retains that immutable
selection for the lifetime of the process. Reader, writer, and lease workers receive
the resolved selection explicitly; they never resolve the connection again. A
different selection in the same process is refused. Restart the process after
changing the connection or engine.

Offline port commands scope their source and target selections to each worker
task, including resource cleanup, so reusing an idle worker does not change the
Gateway's process selection.

Stores without PostgreSQL support still use SQLite. Incognito storage remains memory-only.
The supported PostgreSQL families are:

- **Shared state:** runtime storage, bidirectional database ports, and
  matched backups. The provider covers the selected `state/openclaw.sqlite` and
  retained Voice Call state roots, including explicitly configured store paths
  and disabled plugin entries. Matrix account/token roots are excluded from this
  provider; their discovery and custody belong to the Matrix account-root lane.
- **Agent databases:** fresh agent stores, including shared-main auth and explicit
  agent directories, use the selected engine through the existing agent workers.
  Transcript payloads are stored as plain JSON on PostgreSQL. Transcript text search
  uses the engine's admitted full-text capability and requires `unaccent`.
  Memory indexing remains unavailable until the memory owner supports PostgreSQL;
  requests fail with `DATABASE_SEARCH_CAPABILITY_UNAVAILABLE`.
  Existing SQLite agent stores cannot switch engines; agent ports and backup
  providers are not available yet. PostgreSQL agent schemas support current-version
  bootstrap only and reject schema drift before exposing the store.
- **Workboard:** runtime storage, bidirectional database ports, and matched backups.
- **Logbook:** runtime frames, batches, observations, cards, and standups;
  bidirectional database ports; and matched backups. Frame images remain local
  file artifacts under `logbook/frames`. Ports preserve their stored paths and
  leave the files in place. Backups include that directory alongside the database
  export and anchor; retain it when restoring or moving an installation.
- **Team Reports:** saved reports, person-day counts, and run history;
  bidirectional database ports; and matched backups. Collected activity is
  session-local scratch and is not exported or backed up.

A supported store never silently falls back to SQLite when its PostgreSQL
connection or admission fails.

Doctor can acquire offline maintenance custody and run data-only state migrations
on PostgreSQL. A live or unverifiable Gateway owner still prevents maintenance;
state writes use the existing PostgreSQL writer advisory lock. Registered state
schema migrations retain a full, exact state-family backup and matching anchor
before the version runner begins. Each migration supplies its predecessor backup
descriptor; a missing descriptor refuses the migration. The engine validates the exact
destination schema before commit and publication. Failed migrations roll back
transactionally, while their `.postgres.bak` exports remain available for recovery.

Use `openclaw database port` to move existing supported data between engines.
Changing `database.engine` alone does not migrate existing data. Omitting
`database` preserves the SQLite default, so ordinary updates require no
configuration or data migration.

Existing SQLite shared state and agent databases refuse a PostgreSQL selection and name
`openclaw database port` as the migration path. The port command handles
current-schema shared state, Workboard, Logbook, and Team Reports. Upgrade older
shared state with `openclaw doctor --fix` using a compatible binary before porting.
Agent porting is not available yet; keep existing agent stores on SQLite.
Do not remove existing data to switch engines.

## Search on PostgreSQL

The experimental engine search contract supports native PostgreSQL full text,
literal trigram contains, and exact cosine search. Agent transcript text search
uses this contract; agent memory still follows the support matrix above.
It does not enable PostgreSQL for an unported store.

For a store that declares search indexes, install these extensions in the
database before opening it. The default extension namespace is `public`:

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent WITH SCHEMA public;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm WITH SCHEMA public;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector WITH SCHEMA public;
```

`unaccent` is required for full text, `pg_trgm` for a declared trigram index,
and `vector` for semantic search. Extensions are database-wide; the store's
schema declaration identifies their namespace when it differs from `public`.
The engine checks availability and privileges once at store admission. It never
installs extensions automatically. An unavailable capability refuses admission
with its extension name and operator SQL; it does not return empty search results
or switch storage engines. Extension installation may require a database
administrator. The runtime role needs `CREATE` in the store schema, or database
`CREATE` privilege when bootstrapping a new schema, plus ownership/access to its
tables, indexes, functions, and text-search configuration.

The existing explicit keyword-only memory setting is `memory.search.provider: "none"`
(or the corresponding agent-specific override). The engine's keyword-only schema
requires no pgvector extension and exposes no vector capability. The memory owner's
PostgreSQL integration is pending; this setting does not yet enable memory indexing. Disabling only the native vector
index is not a PostgreSQL JavaScript-scan fallback. An embedding-provider failure
does not silently authorize keyword-only PostgreSQL admission.

Full text uses a named `simple` plus `unaccent` configuration, a stored generated
`tsvector`, and GIN. Queries bind literal terms and compile conjunctions,
disjunctions, adjacent phrases, and final-lexeme prefixes. User text is never
interpreted as PostgreSQL query operators. Ranking uses `ts_rank_cd` with
normalization 2: scores are engine-local, higher is better, and ordering differs
from SQLite BM25. Tokenization also differs for punctuation, compound words, and
Unicode. Snippets use `ts_headline` only after a materialized, bounded candidate
selection, with a word budget of 2–48, a character cap of 500, and empty highlight markers. Trigram
contains uses its own GIN index and escaped literal `ILIKE`; it is not a universal
fallback for full-text queries.

Semantic search uses exact float32 `vector(n)` cosine distance, with model and
source eligibility in the same query before ordering and limit. The canonical
embedding remains its original little-endian binary64 BLOB; source-transaction
triggers maintain the derived float32 projection. Exact vectors support up to
16,000 dimensions. A dimension change requires a matching schema and a derived
index rebuild. There is no ANN, HNSW, IVFFlat, half-precision storage, or transfer
of the PostgreSQL corpus into JavaScript for per-query scoring.

Generated columns, GIN indexes, vector projection tables, trigger functions, and
the named text-search mappings participate in the store's exact schema-drift
fingerprint. Rebuilds run under the owning writer transaction. PostgreSQL search
remains experimental while product-flow conformance and agent storage cutover
are completed.

Managed-service documentation lists pgvector for Amazon RDS, Google Cloud SQL,
Neon, and Supabase, but this is not a tenant availability guarantee. RDS support
depends on the instance patch and extension version; Cloud SQL versions vary by
PostgreSQL major; Neon requires per-database enablement and version verification;
Supabase's setup guide does not guarantee a numeric version. Verify all required
extensions and privileges for the actual database.

## Port existing stores

Stop the Gateway first, through the service owner that normally manages it, and
stop embedded agents using the same state directory. The command refuses a live
owner and never stops or restarts services for you. Configure
`database.postgres.connection` before porting to PostgreSQL, leaving the current
`database.engine` unchanged until the command switches it.

```bash
openclaw database port --to postgres --dry-run
openclaw database port --to postgres
```

Port, backup, restore, and fingerprint operations share one database-family
provider registry. Each provider resolves its stores and supplies the generated
schema descriptor and expected PostgreSQL catalog. **Shared state, Workboard,
Logbook, and Team Reports are registered families.** Agent and Matrix-root
support are not enabled by this registry yet. An unrecognized PostgreSQL anchor
refuses the operation and names the supported families.
For separately installed plugins such as Team Reports, operations load the
selected installed plugin's schema and admission API. Keep the matching plugin
installed for port, backup, and restore. Preflight does not require absent
optional plugins.

The command inventories existing shared state, Workboard, Logbook, and Team Reports stores,
including disabled plugin stores. A real SQLite-to-PostgreSQL port initializes
missing shared state before capture so the config writer uses the same selected
store after the switch. It does not create missing plugin stores or port agent
databases. A dry run checks read-only
prerequisites and reports checks that still require private migration, copying,
or a PostgreSQL privilege probe. It creates no manifest, migrated copy, or target
namespace. Add `--json` for machine-readable results without connection strings
or row payloads.

The real operation retains exact original database and config captures under
`<stateDir>/recovery/database-port/<operation-id>/`. SQLite originals are verified
snapshots with WAL changes settled. PostgreSQL originals include a matched
anchor and exact SQLite export; these captures retain current rows without the
user-backup sanitizer. Config captures include the root file and its includes.
Keep this directory private and retain the complete set. Former PostgreSQL
namespaces are not dropped automatically.

All destination stores are privately migrated and verified before publication.
The command replaces each store atomically, switches config last while preserving
SecretRefs, environment references, and includes, then archives its completed
manifest with the captures. After success, start the Gateway through its service
owner.

An interrupted operation keeps startup blocked by
`<stateDir>/recovery/database-port/manifest.json`. Keep the Gateway stopped and
use that active manifest with one of:

```bash
openclaw database port --resume <stateDir>/recovery/database-port/manifest.json
openclaw database port --rollback <stateDir>/recovery/database-port/manifest.json
```

Resume revalidates the captured evidence and finishes the interrupted operation.
Rollback restores the entire original store and config set. These options are
mutually exclusive and cannot be combined with `--to` or `--dry-run`. Completed,
archived manifests are not an undo command after runtime has resumed.

To return to SQLite without losing writes accepted after a successful port, stop
the Gateway and run a new reverse port:

```bash
openclaw database port --to sqlite --dry-run
openclaw database port --to sqlite
```

Reverse-port before downgrading through a raw package manager such as npm, pnpm,
or Homebrew: those paths bypass `openclaw update` engine compatibility checks.
An old SQLite capture is historical and does not contain later PostgreSQL writes.
See the [CLI reference](/cli#database).

## Several Gateways on one PostgreSQL server

Several independent installations can share one PostgreSQL server. Each
installation must have its own state directory and exactly one Gateway.
Sharing one installation across Gateways, including failover and active-active
operation, is not supported: each store has one live owner.

### Recommended: one database per Gateway

Use a separate PostgreSQL database and connection DSN for each Gateway. This
provides the strongest isolation between installations. Install the required
search extensions in **each database**, as described in
[Search on PostgreSQL](#search-on-postgresql); extensions installed in one database
are not available in another. Each installation can use the default
`database.postgres.schemaPrefix` because their databases are separate.

A database administrator creates the databases and may need to install extensions.
The runtime role needs `CONNECT` and database `CREATE` privilege to bootstrap its
store schemas, plus ownership/access to its store objects and `USAGE` on the
extension schema.

### One database with separate namespaces

Give each Gateway a distinct `database.postgres.schemaPrefix`, such as
`installation_a` and `installation_b`. Each store gets a separate anchor UUID and
namespace; its writer advisory lock uses that UUID. Keep each local anchor with
its matching PostgreSQL namespace. Pairing one installation's anchor with another
installation's namespace refuses admission. Changing the configured prefix does
not move an existing anchor.

Install `unaccent`, `pg_trgm`, and `vector` once in the shared database's `public`
schema (or the explicitly declared extension schema). All installations reuse
those extensions; admission checks them and never recreates them. Text-search
configurations are schema-qualified, and generated columns, indexes, vector
projections, and functions belong to each store namespace.

The runtime role needs `CONNECT` on the shared database and database `CREATE`
privilege to bootstrap namespaces, plus ownership/access to its store objects and
`USAGE` on the extension schema. Use separate roles and schema grants when
installations also need a PostgreSQL permission boundary; schema prefixes alone
do not restrict a role's access.

## Isolation and durability

One Gateway owns each store. PostgreSQL does not enable multiple active owners of one store,
external writers, replication management, or connection-pool management.

Writers use `READ COMMITTED` and a transaction-scoped advisory lock derived from
the store identity. Every PostgreSQL write, including a single statement, uses
the adapter's `runTransaction` so it retains that lock and publishes its write
token. A single-statement read may use autocommit; multi-statement snapshot reads
use `REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY`. Connections
set `synchronous_commit=off` to match SQLite WAL with `synchronous=NORMAL`: a
server or operating-system crash can lose recently acknowledged commits. Backups
and recovery must account for that durability policy. The adapter sets generous
lock and statement timeouts once during connection setup; operations do not
change timeout settings individually.

## Anchors and backups

A PostgreSQL store keeps a small SQLite anchor at its usual local database path.
The anchor records the store UUID, engine, and PostgreSQL schema. New schemas use
`<schemaPrefix>_<store>_<uuid-prefix>`; moving the anchor preserves the identity.
PostgreSQL schema metadata must match the anchor's store UUID and expected schema
version. Admission checks run once per physical store per process load, and
workers and handles reuse the admitted facts. Confirmed commits and uncertain
commit outcomes invalidate cached store facts through the anchor's write token.

PostgreSQL catalog admission captures column types, nullability, exact defaults,
keys, CHECK expressions, index definitions (including partial predicates), and
trigger definitions and function bodies from the server in one consistent read.
Bootstrap and migrations record a fingerprint of these PostgreSQL-deparsed facts,
a hash of the generated DDL for the active schema, and the server major version.
Startup compares the live fingerprint and the build's DDL hash with that record.
A mismatch refuses admission and names the recovery step. After a server-major
upgrade, admission compares the live catalog with generated DDL in a temporary
namespace, removes that namespace, and records the new fingerprint only on a
match. Unsealed pilot/ported stores receive the same one-time comparison. These facts are separate from the anchor's SQLite
catalog. Ordinary data commits retain schema admission; schema owners publish
replacement facts after committed DDL. Optional SQLite WAL, checkpoint, and
page-reclamation work does not apply to PostgreSQL. Explicit SQLite integrity,
repair, and file-snapshot requests refuse with a PostgreSQL recovery instruction.

Runtime PostgreSQL queries run in workers. Physical open and boot migration code
may use the synchronous `withEngineStoreAdmission` scope from
`openclaw/plugin-sdk/database-engine-worker-runtime`; retaining a connection after
that scope ends does not authorize main-thread queries. The callback must remain
synchronous. Close remains available to settle resources. The store owner supplies
`openEngineStore` with `inspectSqlite(): { hasExistingData, hasEngineAnchor }`,
so partially initialized stores are also protected from an accidental engine
switch. See the canonical
[`admission scope`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/infra/database-engine/admission-scope.ts)
and [`engine opener`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/blob/main/src/infra/database-engine/open.ts).

Use `openclaw backup create` to capture PostgreSQL stores together with the
SQLite stores that still hold the rest of the installation. PostgreSQL backup
requires the Gateway stopped. If it is running, the command refuses: “stop
through the service owner, then rerun.” It never stops the Gateway automatically.
This requirement also applies to generic local snapshots and Git backups when
their selected source is PostgreSQL. `openclaw backup sqlite` refuses a PostgreSQL
anchor and directs you to `openclaw backup create`.

A PostgreSQL backup contains a portable SQLite export image, the original anchor,
and a format-2 manifest. The export reads one `REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY` snapshot,
then applies the existing user-backup sanitizer before compaction and hashing.
The manifest records the backup profile, engine, store UUID, schema versions,
active fragments, allocation facts, artifact sizes, and hashes. It never records
the connection DSN. Active optional fragments come from the source catalog,
not from enabled-plugin configuration; a missing required fragment dependency
refuses the copy. Restore re-admits that same fragment set. Canonical triggers
are installed after loading rows, while declared derived projections are omitted
from copying and rebuilt by their owner before verification. Unknown triggers
and views refuse the operation. Owners can migrate an older SQLite source only
in the operation's private copy; the original capture remains intact. Shared-state
ports require the current schema and preserve absent optional fragments, including
Doctor-owned deletion history. Its persisted projection columns and tables are
canonical data, so they are retained rather than rebuilt. Exact captures keep
secrets and transient rows; user exports apply the existing shared-state sanitizer.
Restore uses normal owner admission, including PostgreSQL catalog drift checks.

Preserve the complete matched set: an anchor alone contains
no PostgreSQL rows. Existing format-1 SQLite backups remain readable.

PostgreSQL restore verifies the matched set, loads a fresh owned namespace, and
publishes its matching anchor only after verification. Keep the displaced
namespace until recovery is confirmed. User backups follow the usual
sanitization and credential-exclusion policy; they are not exact updater recovery
captures. See [Backups](/install/backups) and [Backup CLI](/cli/backup).

## Updates and target compatibility

Updates preserve each store's physical engine. Before database mutation, the
installed updater captures PostgreSQL rows and their matching anchor without
sanitization, alongside the existing exact SQLite captures. Recovery restores
PostgreSQL into a fresh owned namespace and publishes its matched anchor; the
migrated namespace remains available until recovery is confirmed. Changed state
or uncertain custody prevents automatic restore and retains the captures for
recovery. An update never silently ports a store or falls back to SQLite.

Release packages declare supported engines in the optional
`openclaw.databaseEngines` array in `package.json`, next to
`openclaw.updateAdmissionProtocol`. An absent array means `["sqlite"]`; the
admission protocol remains `1`. Only installations with a physical non-SQLite
store use this additional check. A target without `postgres` is refused before
mutation with a remedy: reverse-port to SQLite with the current compatible binary,
or stay on the current version. SQLite-only installations keep their existing
admission behavior. The installed driver owns this check; a candidate cannot
repair an older driver. See [Update admission](/cli/update#candidate-owned-admission).

## Limits and recovery

Startup checks the fixed `recovery/database-port/manifest.json` under the selected
state directory before CLI config snapshots and again after acquiring fresh
Gateway or embedded-writer custody. An absent manifest or valid completed
manifest permits startup. An incomplete, unreadable, malformed, or unknown
manifest refuses startup and identifies the recovery artifact. These checks do
not open a database. Keep the manifest and its captured originals intact, then
use `openclaw database port --resume <manifest>` or `--rollback <manifest>`.

Fresh stores bootstrap from generated PostgreSQL DDL at the current store schema
version. Older stores run owner-supplied consecutive forward migrations under the
PostgreSQL writer transaction and advisory lock. A failure rolls back the pending
steps and their metadata; admitted facts publish only after commit. Each step
compares its result with the generated destination DDL in a temporary namespace
before recording the DDL hash and live catalog fingerprint. A missing migration
refuses admission. Newer stores require a compatible binary, or a reverse port
with a compatible binary before downgrade. Never edit schema metadata to bypass
admission.

The generated shared-state `state.postgres.sql` and `fragment-*.postgres.sql`
files contain runtime DDL only. Their caller supplies the transaction and
`search_path`; no second wrapped copy is generated. For manual readiness checks,
see [applying the generated state DDL](/reference/database-schemas/storage-changes#shared-state-postgresql-schema-generation).
The generated agent DDL likewise leaves the transaction and search path to its owner.

PostgreSQL text cannot contain NUL characters. Values containing NUL fail with an
engine error. Search/vector capabilities remain store-specific; selecting an
engine does not add PostgreSQL support to an unported store.

| Failure                                   | Next step                                                                                               |
| ----------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Missing or unresolved connection secret   | Configure `database.postgres.connection` and verify the SecretRef provider is available to the Gateway. |
| Unreachable PostgreSQL server             | Check the DSN, network access, role permissions, and server availability.                               |
| Store UUID mismatch                       | Restore the matching anchor and PostgreSQL schema; do not pair an anchor with another store.            |
| Newer schema or missing forward migration | Use a compatible OpenClaw binary; reverse-port with that binary before a downgrade.                     |
| Gateway running during PostgreSQL backup  | Stop through the service owner, then rerun the backup command.                                          |
| Update target lacks PostgreSQL support    | Stay on the current version or reverse-port with the current compatible binary before retrying.         |

## Observe database work

The engine boundary publishes Node.js `diagnostics_channel` events on
`openclaw.database.statement` and `openclaw.database.request`. Subscriptions are
isolate-local: statement events are emitted in the database worker, and request
events on the host. Subscribe in each process or worker you want to measure:

```js

channel("openclaw.database.statement").subscribe((event) => {
  // Count by event.engine, or inspect event.durationMs and event.outcome.
});
```

Each connection execution call emits one statement event. Compound `exec` or
query SQL produces one event carrying the normalized compound text; observation
does not split SQL or execute extra queries. Each worker `scope.execute` request,
connection open, and connection close emits one host-side request event.
Both include `engine` (`"sqlite"` or `"postgres"`),
`threadId`, `outcome` (`"ok"` or `"error"`), and `durationMs`. Statement events
also include normalized `sql` with literals redacted; neither event includes
bindings. Request events count the worker boundary separately from the statements
that the request executes. This lets census tools compare both engines without
inferring them from SQL. When no subscriber is present, the boundary skips timing,
SQL normalization, and event construction.

See [Database schemas](/reference/database-schemas) for store ownership and schema
contracts, and [Configuration reference](/gateway/configuration-reference) for
the rest of the Gateway configuration.

---

# Database schemas
Source: https://docs.openclaw.ai/reference/database-schemas

OpenClaw stores control-plane state in the shared state database and agent data in one database per agent. SQLite is the default; fresh agent stores also support the [experimental PostgreSQL engine](/reference/database-engines). SQLite schema migrations run forward when a database opens. PostgreSQL agent schemas currently support bootstrap only. Older OpenClaw builds refuse databases written by a newer schema.

For runtime contributors, start with
[database access in workers](/reference/database-schemas/worker-access): execution
owners, admission once per load, scoped write receipts, memory-only final
authority guards, and session actors. The
[migration inventory](/reference/database-schemas/worker-access-inventory)
records remaining main-thread call sites and the ratchet that prevents growth.

PostgreSQL shared-state generation requires PostgreSQL 16+, preserves lazy feature
fragments, and keeps engine schema versions in lockstep. See
[shared-state schema generation](/reference/database-schemas/storage-changes#shared-state-postgresql-schema-generation)
for catalog equivalence and the portable v22 identity columns.

The Gateway process is the single owner of every OpenClaw database and its state.
Its workers and native handles share that ownership. Committed write receipts
invalidate in-process row caches before their next use; a cache without complete
writer coverage must use a direct read instead. Runtime reads do not probe foreign
commits with `PRAGMA data_version`, version observations, or foreign-observation
scopes. SQLite statements outside an open read transaction already see committed
data. A single-statement read needs no explicit transaction; multi-statement reads
keep a transaction when their results require one consistent snapshot.
CLI, Doctor, cron, and plugin child processes must route mutations through the
Gateway or acquire exclusive ownership while it is stopped. First admission,
migration, repair, and final live-authority checks retain their existing owners.

Admitted updater mutation guards read current recovery rows directly rather than
starting a synchronous snapshot subprocess for every effect. Explicit
artifact-preserving inspection still uses private snapshots. Initial recovery
admission, finalization checks, executor authority, and refusal of newly committed
recovery remain unchanged; no recovery decision is cached across an await.

Before Doctor's pre-repair capture admits live SQLite reads, maintenance reuses
the source content revision while the database, WAL, and journal file identities,
sizes, and nanosecond modification/change timestamps remain unchanged. Capture
checks still evaluate current custody, quarantine, and update admission each time;
the final metadata observation invalidates cached rows even when a write happens
during revision selection. Changed source files require a fresh revision and ledger read. Backup ordering,
stored bytes, schemas, and rollback behavior are unchanged.

Agent deletion status is loaded on first admission and retained per agent in the
physical shared database's process-owned facts. Journal writers publish pending,
completed, and removed status at commit through the existing worker fact transport;
rollback preserves the previous status. Session admission reuses this fact and the
deletion owner's queue closure instead of reading the journal on every turn.
Synchronous runtime guards reuse the same committed fact rather than copying the
shared database for each check. Guards inside a native transaction still read
that transaction's current journal, including its uncommitted changes.
Restart loads persisted tombstones again. Destructive cleanup retains its current
journal-authority checks; schema, retention, and update behavior are unchanged.

Once Gateway startup holds exclusive state ownership, it inspects the previous
Gateway lease directly in a read-only worker instead of copying the shared
database. Fresh or unverifiable owners still prevent startup; Doctor's schema
repair admission keeps its private snapshot on SQLite. PostgreSQL maintenance
inspects the lease through an admitted state reader without a file snapshot.

Borrowed worker transactions obtain their initial host grant before `BEGIN
IMMEDIATE`; writes with domain or publication facts still revalidate those facts
at commit. Transcript-index preflight and sweep instead admit one bounded derived
maintenance effect before attempting a nonblocking `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`. They reread
all source rows inside that transaction and make no host requests while holding
the writer lock. Contention returns pending work to the existing yielding drain,
which obtains fresh grants on its next attempt. The final grant linearizes this
internal maintenance against subsequent revocation; it is never retained across
asynchronous work or a lock wait. Schemas, stored formats, retention, permissions,
and update behavior are unchanged.

Update-history workers bound commit-admission waits to one second. On timeout,
the transaction rolls back before the same worker command retries, preserving
FIFO ordering and rereading the current rows. Fresh admission waits outside
`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, leaving the serving Gateway's writer free while the updater
host is busy. Authority refusals and uncertain rollback outcomes are not retried;
required update and recovery records retain their existing durability.

Channel-identity writes use the same one-second admission budget at transaction
entry and commit, with at most three attempts. Entry admission waits before
`BEGIN`; a commit timeout rolls back before retrying with fresh authority and
current rows. Exhaustion names the failed operation and directs the operator to
`openclaw gateway status --deep` before retrying. Final commit authorization stays
inside the transaction until the remaining authority owners can transfer their checks.

Database-fact readers do not contact the host inside a transaction. Missing writer
registrations or unpublished facts remain unknown until the transaction closes;
schema readers retain their conservative snapshot validation. The next read
outside the transaction can refresh those facts through the existing owner.

Native SQLite initialization reads the loaded library's version and extension
capability in one query before admitting real state databases. Auth-profile
readers install their lock-wait timeout at connection open.
On first Gateway startup, a version-zero database containing only recognized
native bootstrap tables is completed before runtime history is read. This uses
the existing schema owner and preserves the native rows; it does not repair
historical installations during ordinary startup.
Quarantine decision readers and writers set their existing lock-wait timeout at connection
open. The quarantine store's format and each target's decision are loaded once
per physical store. Record and clear operations publish the committed decision
through the existing in-process admission facts, including absence, so ordinary
guards do not repeat the durable lookup. Explicit Doctor inspection reads disk,
and recorded refusals still validate their file generation. Quarantine rows retain
their pathname scope, and aliases still share physical format, schema, and integrity facts.
The persisted schema, WAL safety, and recovery behavior are unchanged.

Agent database opens apply private file and directory modes. Warm reads and writes
reuse the open connection without inspecting or repairing those modes again;
permission drift is repaired on the next open or by explicit maintenance. Retained
operations also reuse their admitted file identity. A replacement after admission
does not redirect that operation to the replacement file; the next admission or
open detects it through the database lifecycle owner. Commit authority checks and
Doctor's explicit verification remain in place.

Fresh agent databases install the current canonical schema directly, without
running legacy migration discovery or repairing indexes that were just created.
After the creation transaction commits, the schema owner publishes the admitted
catalog and canonical-validation facts for later opens and workers. Tracked DDL
and rollback still invalidate those facts; existing databases retain their first
admission and migration checks. Connection lock timeouts are assigned through
the shared per-handle owner so repeated setup does not repeat the PRAGMA.
Schemas, stored bytes, and upgrade or downgrade behavior are unchanged.

Chat input actors reuse their native owner’s admitted physical identity and
canonical location, without queuing another writer reservation just to acquire
the actor. Cold owners still prepare their database identity first. Captured
session reads constrain the same physical file; actual input writes retain FIFO
admission and current authority checks.

Managed writes publish committed facts before their public observers. Private
receipts distinguish explicit absence from incomplete coverage and preserve known
commits independently of reply delivery. See
[committed facts and completeness](/reference/database-schemas/worker-access#committed-facts-and-completeness)
for ordering, rollback, and the writer families that still retain native guards.

SQLite format, schema-version, integrity, required-index, and table-existence
validation runs once per physical database per process load. A regular
`<database>.seal` file can carry admitted facts across clean restarts: the owner
writes it after a successful `TRUNCATE` checkpoint and native close, and unlinks
it before the next write. Startup reuses it only when its checksum, schema
identity, device, inode, stable birthtime, size, and nanosecond modification time
match, journals are absent or empty, and full verification is at most seven days
old. A hit skips startup snapshot, readiness, schema, and integrity inspection,
including post-ready scans. The plain checksum-protected write needs no rename
or fsync protocol; an incomplete seal falls back to full validation.

Admitted facts are shared with all workers and handles while the database is open.
Final close releases their in-memory payloads; a clean-close seal restores validated
facts on reopen without SQL. A close that cannot seal requires fresh admission.
File identity uses volume, inode, and stable
birthtime captured once with `fstat` on the retained admission descriptor, not SQL.
Admission lookups and established borrowers reuse those shared facts without
checking the pathname again. Native open and reopen still identify replacement
files, and creation witnesses retain their physical file check. A replaced or
restored file needs fresh admission. Migration and repair owners validate their
changes and publish new facts after successful DDL settlement. Doctor and explicit
verification retain full checks, and observed corruption still revokes admission.
Silent corruption with unchanged metadata is outside the seal's guarantee and
is caught by normal SQLite access or the next full verification. See
[clean-close seal and integrity checks](/reference/database-schemas/integrity-and-recovery#integrity-checks)
for the crash argument, verification interval, and maintenance behavior.

Shared-state and agent read-only connections reuse bounded prepared statements
under their native connection lifecycle. Prepared-statement reuse alone does not
retain query results. Schema-fact lookups use the process's admitted facts without
SQL. Writer receipts invalidate cached row results across connections without
querying `data_version`, `schema_version`, `user_version`, or the catalog again.
Current-row authority checks remain at their effect boundaries. Cached rows inside
an active SQLite snapshot use that snapshot's identity and the connection's local
mutation revision. They never carry a current committed-write revision or become
reusable after the snapshot ends. Autocommit caches use the owning writer's receipts.
Closing a connection clears its prepared statements and row caches. Confirmed close
retains the physical database's completed validation facts for later opens in the
same process. Explicit retirement closes the host identity descriptor only after
all sibling native handles have drained, preserving their POSIX locks.

Shared-state commands load their registered domain directly. The remaining command
runtime loads only when an operation needs it, so workers serving registered
operations alone do not retain unrelated command modules. Preparation still
finishes before synchronous database execution; writer admission and receipts
stay with their existing owners.

The shared-state reader pool keeps its first worker warm for the normal handle
idle timeout. Surplus readers retire after 30 seconds idle and restart on demand.
Retirement uses the pool's existing task and native-resource settlement so an
active read or retained lease is not interrupted.

Durable usage refreshes publish rollups in bounded transactions instead of one
writer request per transcript. A batch flushes after 50 transcripts, 1 MiB of
prepared payload, or one second of scanning, checked between whole transcripts;
one large transcript may exceed the byte or time limit. Refresh completion always
flushes the remaining batch. Fresh checkpoints remain untouched, and a failed or
canceled scan leaves uncommitted derived totals for the next refresh. Persisted
rollups, partitions, schemas, and report totals keep their existing format.

Transcript history and search lanes likewise retire surplus workers after 30
seconds idle. Each lane keeps one worker until its existing five-minute idle
retirement, which waits for logical reader leases to be released. Surplus
retirement preserves those leases and waits for active tasks; a later concurrent
read starts another worker on demand.

Canonical auth reads pass a compact projection of the live owner's schema facts
(user version and the two auth table classifications) to the isolated child. The
child reads current credential rows through its bounded native reader pool without
repeating connection setup or schema admission on each request. Retained readers
are bound to the request's admitted physical identity; the parent joins child
cleanup before database deletion. Cold, snapshot, and artifact-preserving reads
still admit their own database; owner DDL invalidates the next projection, and a
replacement physical file cannot borrow the previous file's reader or facts.

Synchronous plugin discovery inside workers likewise borrows the existing
shared-state reader pool. Each pass reads current rows, while the native reader
and its admission survive until worker cleanup or idle expiry. Main-thread
one-shot reads and artifact-preserving snapshots keep their scoped lifetimes.

Worker dispatch carries snapshots prepared by the admission owner when it publishes
facts or writer custody. Unchanged requests reuse the registry revision without
scanning every database or rebuilding fact maps. Shared revocation cells still
invalidate transferred facts immediately; retirement removes the published snapshot.
This changes no schema, stored bytes, or update behavior.

Shared-state content-version checks reuse the physical database's admitted version
facts across open handles and workers. Ordinary commits, transactions, and closing
one of several connections do not force another marker read. The migration owner publishes replacement
facts with its committed schema. Observed DDL without replacement facts expires
the content-version admission: an unchanged catalog shape does not prove that the
`config_machine_state` marker survived. The next owner lookup validates it once,
and later opens reuse the result. A historical snapshot keeps its own marker facts;
publication requires a positive match with the current committed admission. Each
caller still applies its published-version floor. Schema versions, stored bytes,
and upgrade or downgrade behavior are unchanged.

New agent readers reuse the process's schema admission. Shared-state worker reads
consume writer-invalidated cache facts or current rows without a freshness probe.
Point transcript statistics, mutation clocks, pending-archive checks, and
hot/cold watermarks use a single statement's snapshot; composite reads retain
their read transaction, and hot transcript reads reuse an existing transaction
without a nested savepoint. Yielding write admission restores its temporary busy
timeout once, immediately after acquiring the write transaction, and carries an
inherited lock deadline without rereading the connection's timeout. FIFO,
lock-wait budgets, schemas, stored data, and update behavior are unchanged.

Activity-summary batches read metadata, ancestry, and bounded messages in one
native snapshot. Transcript appends fold an existing window's recency into their
final mutation-watermark write; rejected duplicates still record attempt recency.
Connections retain their owner-set busy timeout and skip unchanged assignments.
The audit writer retains the earliest expiry and skips empty pruning until it is
due, invalidating that fact on rollback or maintenance. Audit retention, transcript
timestamp semantics, schemas, and update behavior are unchanged.

The admitted catalog includes index names and trigger definitions alongside tables.
Stored-session validation consumes these definitions without another catalog scan.
First required-index admission shares the schema contract reader's batched metadata snapshot
instead of querying each table and index separately. Shadowed PRAGMA names retain
native inspection during that validation. Authorization, initial drift detection,
transactional repair, and integrity checks remain with their existing owners.
First-use schema owners skip additive DDL only when all their tables and indexes
are present in the published facts. Missing objects use the existing installation
transaction, which publishes the new schema facts on commit; rollback cannot
publish a schema that did not commit. Admission publications use the active
connection’s transaction state and the store’s shared publication anchor, so
PostgreSQL transactions also defer facts until commit and discard them on rollback.
Ordinary connection replacement and data
commits do not repeat schema validation. Schemas, stored bytes, and update behavior
are unchanged.

Audit lifecycle bindings, node-worker launch companions, worker placement moves,
skill-library and worker-environment preparation, goal receipts, Board preparation,
and memory origin/provenance preparation reuse these admitted objects even on
their first use of a warm connection. Redundant DDL would revoke retained profile
authority, so an existing table is not recreated just to prepare a store. Retired
memory triggers are removed only when present; imported memory rows still receive
their existing provenance backfill. Private update and Windows workspace lease
owners likewise create their table only when missing. No schema version, stored
shape, upgrade, or downgrade behavior changes.

Shared-state bootstrap checks native table options once after installing the
canonical schema. When every ordinary table is already STRICT, it skips legacy
STRICT rebuild planning and duplicate schema installation. Existing non-STRICT
tables still use the transactional migration, and final canonical table and index
validation remains mandatory. Doctor's explicit repair and version refusal are
unchanged; this changes no stored format or upgrade/downgrade contract.

Admitted schema facts survive data-only transaction settlement. Committed write
receipts invalidate cached row facts. A settled write releases its receipt fence
even when an independent read cursor remains open on the same connection. Active
write cursors and explicit transactions retain their fence until settlement.
Rejected writer discovery leaves no native mutation depth behind, so a later
committed write still invalidates cached rows.
This changes no schema, stored data, or update behavior. Transaction-local views of
schema facts end with their SQLite snapshot; the next transaction consumes the
process's published facts without repeating validation.

Progress-card writes reuse the transaction's admitted table facts. The schema owner creates the lazy table only when it is absent and publishes the committed facts for every handle and worker. A rolled-back installation remains absent until the next normal installation transaction. Stored cards, revision tombstones, schema versions, and upgrade or downgrade behavior are unchanged.

The agent-database execution owner retains up to four idle physical-agent executors in least-recently-used order. Borrowing an executor refreshes its independent 30-minute idle timeout; a fifth idle executor evicts the least recently used one. Configuration changes to the agent roster or storage paths leave existing executors to expire normally. Already-admitted work retains its original physical store; new requests resolve the current configuration. Explicit database closure and Gateway shutdown still revoke and drain the existing lifecycle resources. This changes no schema, stored bytes, or update behavior.

Creating an agent database at an admitted absent path revokes the previous file's
retained validation before worker preparation. A recreated file cannot borrow that
proof even if Linux reuses its inode. Ordinary reopen still reuses live proof,
and fresh stores keep their session certification. Receipt identifiers survive
worker transfers so alias publication revokes superseded proof while preserving
acknowledged copies. Later revocation still refuses publication. Schemas, stored
bytes, and update behavior are unchanged.

Retaining an already-open agent handle holds its lifetime without querying SQLite. Writer receipts invalidate its cached row facts; schema facts come from process-wide admission. Session readiness invalidates its clean-store decision when the owning writer changes the store.

The agent ID and role in `schema_meta` describe the physical store's fixed schema
owner. Creation and migration validate and publish these facts for every handle
and worker; ordinary commits do not require another ownership-metadata read.
Observed DDL without owner-published replacement metadata expires that admission,
even when the recreated table has the same definition: its primary row must be
validated once by the next owner lookup. Historical metadata stays with its
snapshot until positively matched to current committed admission. External row
edits do not reassign an admitted store. Live session permissions, lease ownership,
and caller authority retain their current-row checks. Dynamic authorizers retain
native metadata reads. This changes no schema, stored bytes, or update behavior.

Registry discovery reuses successful migration checks for the admitted schema
generation. The minute retention sweep reads deletion history in a worker and
shares one matcher across its agent stores; live deletion status and lifecycle
commit guards still apply. Cron registry retention validates the complete listing
in its reader worker and returns only cron-run entries to the Gateway; ordinary
session metadata stays in the worker. Legacy watch-marker discovery uses an indexed prefix
range. Retention continues as rows age, even without writes; schema, upgrade, and
retention policies are unchanged.

Session row-facts reads reuse an admitted continuation's existing transaction
instead of nesting a savepoint. Reads without an active transaction still open
one so entry metadata, board presence, and transcript watermarks share a snapshot.
Board presence travels in the exact-entry query, including its single-key error
fallback, instead of a separate Board read.

Placement projections read placement, move, pending-result, journal, and environment
facts in one statement per bounded batch. Batches share the existing read
transaction; journal and result-claim checks consume those same snapshot facts.
Optional columns come from admitted schema facts and refresh with that owner.

Placement retirement checks the inventory once at startup, then checks only IDs
changed by placement receipts or session identity mutations. Clean idle passes
perform no retirement reads. Unknown evidence and failed cleanup remain pending
for the existing minute sweep. Config, store topology, and uncertain session
storage publications request a fresh inventory scan. Retirement predicates and
remote environment teardown keep their existing authority checks.

Skills discovery shares installed-plugin inventory facts across the workspaces in
one worker scan. Each new scan starts with a fresh plugin cache, so installed
plugin changes remain visible without rereading the same index for every agent.

Shared-state read operations retain their admission revision through their
synchronous domain read. ACP metadata reuses at most 128 rows per connection
under that revision; writer receipts, schema changes, and close
invalidate reuse. Transactions and pinned or authorizer-controlled reads still
query SQLite. Supplied shared-state writers reuse their selected handle and check
ownership after `BEGIN`, without a duplicate pre-transaction row read or schema
validation.
Stored bytes, schemas, permissions, and update behavior are unchanged.

Exact entry and participant readers retain their last result at the admitted
connection revision. Repeated reads reuse those facts until an owning writer's
receipt, rollback, schema change, or connection retirement invalidates them.
Session revision guards and maintenance snapshots retain their mutation and
snapshot predicates; transaction entry, rollback, and settlement retain their
existing invalidation without foreign-commit probing.
No schema, stored bytes, permissions, or update behavior change.
Returned entries and participant identities remain caller-owned. Transcript
watermark reads select the hot generation and the retained cold or hot sequence
in one statement; hot-only readers keep their existing meaning. These query
changes preserve schemas, stored bytes, live authority, and update behavior.

Display-history readers resolve selected activity anchors by session and event ID,
retaining the sequence fence inside the same read snapshot. These point lookups
use the existing primary key and require no schema or data migration.

Session entry writes batch their saved snapshot fields in one upsert, preserving
per-field revision triggers and rollback.

Entry replacement snapshots carry the transcript watermark alongside the existing
window facts. Metadata writers return that token with their entry postimage;
a transcript mutation in the same transaction supplies its newer committed token.
Publication does not scan the transcript again. Exact message rewrites likewise
return the generation minted by their writer. Detached edits still compare their
prepared payload with the current row before writing. Schemas, stored bytes,
retention, permissions, and update behavior are unchanged.

Primary-session key policy, external-supervision ownership, and the machine-owned
TTS preference path are loaded once for the physical database and shared across
handles and workers. Their owning writers publish committed replacements;
unrelated writes do not invalidate these facts. The Gateway owns runtime writes.
Other processes must use that owner or run while it is stopped, except established
updater handoff, restart-sentinel, and update-finalization writers, which retain their
own lifecycle fences. Ownership claims require exclusive offline custody. Explicit
ownership inspection and Doctor still read the database, and live lifecycle and lease checks
remain at effect boundaries. Cached policy facts do not grant database admission
or continuation authority. Main-key writer publications carry a host revision, so
workers can retain an absent publication without polling after unrelated writes.
Nested workers forward only the host completeness they actually received. The shared
generation layout keeps write receipts in slot 5 and host-publication completeness
in slot 6; these independent witnesses never share a counter.
Present main-key values are data facts: unrelated DDL cannot retire a committed
config postimage. A missing policy row stays with the connection's read revision
until the schema owner's seed or canonical writer makes the policy available.
Uncertain rollback can discard a data fact and require one repair read before reuse.

Concurrent Windows handoff initializers share the existing writer admission lock
until private file publication finishes, preserving the single-link file check
without quarantining another initializer's in-progress publication.

The Mentions Inbox retains its committed head through the same physical owner.
An unchanged head skips snapshot worker dispatch. A changed or uncertain mutation
reads the head and retained sources in one atomic query before resuming its FIFO;
an unknown write outcome never authorizes replay. Session-entry mutation generations
live in JavaScript beside their connection. TEMP triggers observe exact session
and participant writes, and rollback invalidates generations without selecting a
TEMP counter row. Auth-profile readers use admitted catalog facts for tables,
views, and absence instead of querying the catalog for each read. These changes
preserve schemas, stored bytes, durability, retention, permissions, and update behavior.

The device-pair notifier retains an empty subscriber and delivery-receipt state
for its service lifetime, so idle scheduled scans do not reread both stores.
Its own writes across Gateway and agent registries invalidate that fact, including
uncertain outcomes, and service restart reloads it. Active notifications retain
their current subscription checks and delivery receipts; persisted subscriptions
and receipt retention are unchanged.

The Gateway does not schedule daily full-database scans. Startup reuses recent
clean-close seals or performs the required full validation; a seal hit does not
queue a post-ready verification scan. Doctor and explicit verification retain
full checks. See [integrity admission and Doctor maintenance](/reference/database-schemas/integrity-and-recovery#integrity-checks)
for the seven-day verification interval and operator-requested verification.

Gateway startup and restart checks admit only configured agent database targets.
Retained stores for unconfigured agents remain untouched for Doctor to inspect.
An incompatible secondary agent database refuses that agent's sessions with
`openclaw doctor --fix` guidance, without blocking healthy agents or restarting
the Gateway. Shared-state and required system-agent checks remain strict.

Two mechanisms back that contract. CI runs
`scripts/check-native-state-schema-version.mjs`, which fails the build when the
Swift and TypeScript state-database contracts declare different schema versions.
[`openclaw doctor --fix`](/cli/doctor) owns file-to-SQLite migrations and records a
receipt for each one in the shared `migration_runs` and `migration_sources` tables.

Execution step receipts are separate from these persisted import receipts.
A step blocked by an earlier refusal includes optional `originatingRefusal`
fields `stepId`, `code`, and `message` naming the first failure. See
[legacy state migration](/cli/doctor/state-migrations) for how to resolve it.

# Agent schema history
Source: https://docs.openclaw.ai/reference/database-schemas/agent-schema-history

## Agent schema history

**Published in** names the first stable release tag containing each change,
or the first beta tag when no stable release contains it yet. Several schema
changes can first ship together in a release that writes a higher version.
`Unreleased` is reserved for changes absent from both stable and beta tags.
Use the target release's history when planning an upgrade: the installed
version's `openclaw update --dry-run` does not reveal the target's migration plan.
Older builds refuse newer schemas; rollback requires the verified pre-upgrade
backup and its matching build, not just reinstalling the older package.

| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------ |

| 2       | Memory index identity ([#104449](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104449))                                                                                                                                                                    | `v2026.8.1`  |
| 4       | Sessions and transcripts moved into SQLite ([#98236](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/98236))                                                                                                                                                 | `v2026.8.1`  |
